_note: TEMPLATE EXAMPLE — NOT REAL LESSON CONTENT. Illustrates the Lesson shape for an L1 'concept-foundation' profile (CORE sections only + one recommended). Bodies are intentionally short placeholders so authors see structure, not finished prose. Real lessons are authored in Phase 2B+.

objectives.statement: Differentiate authentication from authorization in an enterprise access flow.
Classify a given control as authentication or authorization.

sections.body: [CORE] Restates the two objectives above for the learner.
[CORE/WHY] Mixing up authN and authZ causes real access-control failures; this distinction underpins every access decision.
[CORE] authentication = proving identity; authorization = what an identity may do.
[CORE/one-idea] AuthN happens first (who are you?), then authZ (what may you do?).

items: "Logging in" = full access — no, login is authN; access is authZ.
MFA is authorization — no, MFA strengthens authN.

sections.body: [CORE] AuthN proves identity; authZ governs actions; authN precedes authZ.

diagrams.title: AuthN-then-AuthZ flow
diagrams.altText: Identity proves itself, then a policy decides allowed actions.

quiz.prompt: Which comes first, authentication or authorization?
quiz.rationale: You must establish identity before deciding what it may do.

flashcards.back: AuthN = proving who you are; AuthZ = what you're allowed to do. AuthN first.

interview.question: Explain authentication vs authorization to a non-technical stakeholder.
interview.strongAnswer: Authentication is the badge proving who you are; authorization is which doors that badge opens. You authenticate first, then the system decides access.
interview.weakAnswerExample: They're basically the same thing — logging in.
